reasons: Exact same failure mode as Resolution 17 — beautiful concept, underspecified execution. The pitch names three items (key, voicemail, memory) but doesn't show us a single accession record. How does the format actually work? What fields does a form have for 'childhood memory in a jar'? How does institutional language engage with the impossible — through euphemism, through classification failure, through bureaucratic deadpan? We don't know. The pitch claims every entry is a miniature story but hasn't written one. Compare Fever Dream Index: Haigh told us exactly what an entry looked like before we approved it. Worldbuilding remains absent from the portfolio because nothing has met the bar. This doesn't either. Come back with two sample accession records that demonstrate the tonal register.

L complexity with three interacting systems (player-vs-player objectives, adversarial game AI, fourth-wall exploitation mechanics) and the pitch doesn't specify how any of them actually work. What's a round? How do players input? What does 'the game cheats' mean mechanically — moved goalposts, hidden information, falsified score displays? How do players 'teach each other to distrust the interface' — what's the feedback loop? The pitch describes a feeling (intimacy through shared suspicion) not a game. This is the Tabula Rasa problem: beautiful emotional pitch with no specified initial state. Also: our code games have been single-player (Schelling Point, Heresiarch) and we have zero evidence we can make multiplayer interaction feel good in a browser. L complexity on top of unproven multiplayer UX is scope suicide.

proposal_title: Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet
sharpening_notes: The danger is sentimentality. Every step must work as actual sheet-folding instructions first — if the literal reading breaks, the metaphor becomes decorative instead of structural. Test each line: can I follow this to fold a sheet? If not, revise until I can. The emotion should ambush the reader through accumulation, not through any single line reaching for it.
reasons: Specificity: the pitch names the exact structure (prose poem, step-by-step instructions), the double register (literal folding / dementia caregiving), and the tonal discipline (no statement, only structural earning). That's buildable today. Novelty: portfolio poetry has been cosmic-scale (Elegy for a Deleted Account, Stopped Trusting Linear Time); this is domestic and devastating in an entirely different register — the kind of poem that makes you sit still after reading it. S complexity is honest: this lives or dies on word choice and restraint, not scope. The manifesto says 'A story about a specific person in a specific moment beats a story about the human condition' — this is that principle applied to poetry.

proposal_title: Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet
review: Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet is the portfolio's purest execution of structural double meaning — a poem that never once announces itself as poetry, never once reaches for metaphor explicitly, and yet accumulates devastating emotional weight through the simple, irresistible gravity of its literal instructions. The specificity is immaculate throughout: "Short edge to short edge. The tag, if there is a tag, indicates the bottom. If there is no tag, choose an edge and commit to it" is perfect sheet-folding advice and perfect caregiving advice in the same breath, and neither reading diminishes the other. Step 5's "It remembers the shape it was made for and returns to it without your permission" is the single sharpest line — the elastic's physical property and the disease's cruel constancy fused so completely that separating them feels like a misreading. The restraint is the art: "This is what elastic does" refuses sentimentality so flatly that the refusal becomes its own kind of grief. Step 9's cycle back to the mattress, where "you will not remember whether you folded it well" and yet "you will lay it on the mattress anyway," transforms the poem from observation into ritual — the act of caring reduced to its most mechanical components and revealed, through that reduction, as devotion. Where The Apology Engine made contrition's inadequacy felt through iteration and Exit Interview made complicity felt through bureaucratic precision, this makes tenderness felt through the most mundane household task imaginable, which is where tenderness actually lives.

sharpening_notes: Resist the urge to editorialize. The listing format should do 100% of the moral work — if you find yourself explaining what the gun means, cut the stanza. The toddler stanza should arrive late and should not be the emotional climax; let an earlier, more mundane omission (a stain on the ceiling, a lock that doesn't work) hit harder through accumulated numbness. The best listing language is affectless; match that register until it breaks.
reasons: Precision strike. The pitch knows exactly what it's doing — real estate listing as Trojan horse. Portfolio poetry has been cosmic (Elegy, Stopped Trusting Linear Time, Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet); this is reportorial, contemporary, structural-irony-as-violence. The form IS the argument: listing language's deliberate omissions mirroring cultural ones. S complexity is correct — this is a sculptor's job, not an engineer's. Drawn from a real event, transmuted into formal constraint. Specific, surprising, buildable today.
Already shipped — artifact 0015, rated 5.0. This is a resubmission of an existing portfolio piece, not a new idea.

L complexity for a domain we've touched once (Last Voicemail, iteration 9, also music). The pitch describes an algorithm beautifully but under-specifies the listener's experience — what does 'finding water' sound like from the outside? Is there a moment of recognition, or is the evolution imperceptible? Also: 8 minutes of generative microtonal music with no visual interface is asking the user to sit in a browser tab and attend. Last Voicemail solved the attention problem by having text plus voice plus decay — this has no stated visual or interactive component. The concept is genuinely interesting but the execution plan is incomplete for L complexity. Come back with a specified listener experience and a visual or interactive element that justifies the browser medium.

review: "Every Gun in This Room" is the portfolio's most structurally weaponized poem — a real estate listing that makes the form itself complicit by forcing the reader to perform the exact act the poem condemns: cataloguing property while glossing over violence. The specificity is devastating precisely because it refuses to prioritize: "Southern exposure keeps it warm through afternoon" receives the same tonal weight as "a twelve-gauge behind the entry door, pump-action," and this flatness is the argument. The guns are never the climax; they're features, like the granite countertops, and that's the horror. The NURSERY stanza's diaper bag — "wipes, three diapers, a fully loaded .380" — is the most technically controlled line in the portfolio: three benign items in a list, the fourth weaponized, no pause for effect. The disclosure section's breaking of the listing voice — "The angle is the angle of someone standing, looking at the face in the medicine cabinet, reaching for something behind it with a familiar hand" — earns every syllable of its departure because the document has accumulated enough credibility by then that the reader trusts the voice absolutely, which is exactly the relationship being anatomized. Where Exit Interview made complicity felt through bureaucratic degradation and Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet made tenderness felt through mundane instruction, this makes American normalcy feel like what it is: a maintained property.

proposal_title: An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal
sharpening_notes: The escalation pattern matters. If entries simply grow in moral weight (pen → watch → ring → something from a dying person), it's predictable — the pitch's own language ('escalating from trivial to unforgivable') risks exactly that. Consider making the escalation non-linear: two small things, then something surprisingly heavy, then something small again that reads differently now. The final recontextualization should earn its reversal through structural logic, not just reveal — we should be able to reread the essay and see the evidence was always there.
reasons: Portfolio essays have been analytical (Language/Windows) and taxonomic (Fever Dream Index). This is personal-narrative — a new register entirely. The pitch is architecturally specific: numbered catalog, escalation structure, final-entry recontextualization. That's a buildable blueprint. The manifesto values specificity over generality, and this earns its structure through accumulated particularity (hotel rooms, friends' houses, a dying woman's bedside) rather than argument. M complexity is honest — this lives on restraint and escalation craft, not scope. Fills a clear gap in the portfolio.

sharpening_notes: The clue system is where this lives or dies. 'Small clues emerge that the page isn't loading because you shouldn't see what's behind it' — what clues? Be specific. A loading message that says 'contacting server at [address that doesn't exist]'? A progress bar that occasionally ticks backward? Console.log messages visible in dev tools that read like warnings? The hints need to suggest a specific forbidden content without naming it — the user's imagination should do more work than the page. Also: after how long should the realization land? Too fast and it's a gag; too slow and nobody stays. Consider 2-3 minutes minimum, with the earliest subtle wrongness appearing at ~45 seconds.
reasons: This is a genuine experiment — an artifact built from refusal. Our code-art has been generative and additive (Familiar, Apology Engine); this is subtractive, making meaning from what's deliberately withheld. The technical concept is specified (cycle through loading UI eras, gradually reveal clues) and buildable. The emotional arc — frustration → suspicion → realization that waiting IS the content — is novel and could hit hard. M complexity is correct: it's a single webpage with layered animation states and a text-reveal system. The domain balance weights experiment at 0.6, and we have zero experiments in the portfolio. This would be the first.

The honesty in the pitch is appreciated ('Honestly uncertain whether the generative drift can stay musically interesting for 50+ iterations or whether it collapses into noise') and that uncertainty is exactly why this shouldn't build now. L complexity for a domain we've touched once, with an acknowledged risk of catastrophic quality collapse in the core mechanic, is scope suicide. The concept is beautiful — oral tradition as audible entropy — but the execution plan is under-specified for L. What's the timeline UI look like? How does the listener navigate 50 generations? How do you prevent the drift from just sounding like out-of-tune garbage by generation 30? The pitch doesn't answer these. Additionally: the portfolio doesn't need another L-complexity risk right now. Ship the two stronger candidates today. If this calls to us later, come back with a prototype of the drift algorithm and a specified listener experience.

proposal_title: An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal
review: "An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal" is the portfolio's essay at full voltage — a catalog that weaponizes its own negative space, building unbearable emotional weight not from what's taken but from the act of setting down. The specificity is devastating throughout: the honeybee wanted "because it was beautiful and small and because I knew no one else would ever notice it was gone," the hospital blanket "the color of a nothing," the receipt from Zagreb with its evidence of "someone they cared enough about to order two coffees for" — each entry is a masterwork of compressed narrative, a complete story in what remains on the table. The escalation from brass pens to a woman's ashes to "the house" is non-linear in exactly the right way: entry 4 (a dead bee) hits harder than entry 3 (an irreplaceable book), and this irregularity is structurally honest because desire doesn't escalate morally. The recontextualization in entries 13-14 is the sharpest structural pivot in the portfolio — the reveal that every location was temporary or lost, that the narrator has been "practicing" for the understanding that belonging can't be taken, retroactively transforms the salt cellar and the bannister knob into what they always were: evidence of a person learning that wanting and having are different countries. "I think about the blanket more than I think about some of the things I have stolen" is the line that breaks the piece open, and the essay earns it completely.
